questions.explanation:
Highway Engineering | Bituminous Mix Design

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall / Comprehension
  • Concept: Marshall Mix Design method for bituminous concrete.
  • Aim: Identify the correct trends of volumetric and mechanical properties (Stability, Flow, Air Voids, Voids Filled with Bitumen) with an increase in bitumen content.

2. Core Concepts:

The Marshall mix design method evaluates the performance of a bituminous mix by plotting several properties against varying bitumen content. The standard expected trends are:

  1. Marshall Stability: Increases initially, reaches a maximum value, and then decreases. (Initial increase due to binding action of bitumen; subsequent decrease due to thicker bitumen films pushing aggregates apart, reducing interlocking.)
  2. Flow Value: Increases monotonically. (More binder provides more lubrication, making the mix deform more under load.)
  3. Air Voids (\(V_A\)): Decreases monotonically. (As more bitumen is added, it progressively fills the void spaces between aggregate particles.)
  4. Voids Filled with Bitumen (VFB): Increases monotonically. (VFB is the percentage of voids in the mineral aggregate filled with bitumen. More bitumen naturally fills a higher percentage of these voids.)

3. Solution Method & Execution:

OptionStatementVerdict
AStability decreases initially and then increases.❌ False — it increases to a max, then decreases.
BFlow increases monotonically.✅ True
CAir voids (\(V_A\)) increases initially and then decreases.❌ False — it continuously decreases.
DVFB increases monotonically.✅ True

4. Final Answer:

Flow increases monotonically and VFB increases monotonically | Option(s): B, D

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q52
questions.subject: Engineering Mathematics
questions.question:
A 5 cm long metal rod AB was initially at a uniform temperature of \( T_0 \) °C. Thereafter, temperature at both the ends are maintained at 0 °C. Neglecting the heat transfer from the lateral surface of the rod, the heat transfer in the rod is governed by the one-dimensional diffusion equation \( \dfrac{\partial T}{\partial t} = D \dfrac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} \), where \( D \) is the thermal diffusivity of the metal, given as 1.0 cm²/s.
The temperature distribution in the rod is obtained as
\[T(x,t) = \sum_{n=1,3,5...}^{\infty} C_n \sin \dfrac{n\pi x}{5} e^{-\beta n^2 t}, \]
where \( x \) is in cm measured from A to B with \( x = 0 \) at A, \( t \) is in s, \( C_n \) are constants in °C, \( T \) is in °C, and \( \beta \) is in s⁻¹.
The value of \( \beta \) (in s⁻¹, rounded off to three decimal places) is _________________.
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mathematics | Partial Differential Equations

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Length of rod: \(L = 5\) cm
    • 1-D Diffusion equation: \(\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial t} = D\dfrac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2}\)
    • Thermal diffusivity: \(D = 1.0\text{ cm}^2/\text{s}\)
    • Temperature distribution: \(T(x,t) = \displaystyle\sum_{n=1,3,5\ldots}^{\infty} C_n \sin\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\beta n^2 t}\)
  • Aim: Find the value of \(\beta\) in \(\text{s}^{-1}\).

2. Core Concepts:

The given solution \(T(x,t)\) must satisfy the governing 1-D heat diffusion equation. By differentiating the temperature distribution with respect to \(t\) and \(x\), and substituting back into the PDE, we can solve for the unknown constant \(\beta\).

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Differentiate \(T(x,t)\) with respect to \(t\):\[\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \sum_{n=1,3,5\ldots}^{\infty} C_n \sin\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{5}\right) \cdot \left(-\beta n^2\right) e^{-\beta n^2 t}\]
  2. Differentiate \(T(x,t)\) twice with respect to \(x\):\[\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial x} = \sum_{n=1,3,5\ldots}^{\infty} C_n \left(\dfrac{n\pi}{5}\right) \cos\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\beta n^2 t}\]\[\dfrac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} = \sum_{n=1,3,5\ldots}^{\infty} C_n \left(-\dfrac{n^2\pi^2}{25}\right) \sin\!\left(\dfrac{n\pi x}{5}\right) e^{-\beta n^2 t}\]
  3. Substitute into the PDE and compare terms inside the summation for a general \(n\):\[-\beta n^2 = D\left(-\dfrac{n^2\pi^2}{25}\right)\]
  4. Solve for \(\beta\) by cancelling \(-n^2\) from both sides:\[\beta = \dfrac{D\pi^2}{25}\]Given \(D = 1.0\text{ cm}^2/\text{s}\):\[\beta = \dfrac{1.0 \times (3.14159)^2}{25} = \dfrac{9.8696}{25} = 0.394784\text{ s}^{-1}\]
  5. Round off: \(\beta \approx 0.395\text{ s}^{-1}\)

4. Final Answer:

\(\beta = \mathbf{0.395}\text{ s}^{-1}\) | Accepted key range: 0.394 to 0.396

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q53
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A beam is subjected to a system of coplanar forces as shown in the figure. The magnitude of vertical reaction at Support P is _________________ N (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mechanics | Static Equilibrium

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Beam span: \(L = 2.0 + 1.5 + 1.0 + 1.5 = 6.0\text{ m}\)
    • Hinged support at P (\(x = 0\)), Roller support at Q (\(x = 6.0\text{ m}\)).
    • Force 1: \(500\text{ N}\) at \(x = 2.0\text{ m}\), inclined at \(60^\circ\) to horizontal.
    • Force 2: \(200\text{ N}\) at \(x = 3.5\text{ m}\) acting upwards.
    • Bracket at \(x = 4.5\text{ m}\), height \(y = 0.5\text{ m}\); horizontal force \(100\text{ N}\) acting to the right.
  • Aim: Find the magnitude of the vertical reaction at support P (\(V_P\)).

2. Core Concepts:

For a rigid body in static equilibrium, \(\sum M = 0\) about any point. Taking moments about Support Q isolates \(V_P\) (the vertical reaction at Q passes through the pivot and creates zero moment).

Convention: Counter-clockwise (CCW) = positive (+); Clockwise (CW) = negative (−).

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Resolve forces and locate coordinates relative to P:
    • \(500\text{ N}\) at \(x = 2.0\text{ m}\): Vertical component \(F_{y1} = 500\sin(60^\circ) = 433.013\text{ N}\) (downwards).
    • \(200\text{ N}\) at \(x = 3.5\text{ m}\): Acts upwards.
    • \(100\text{ N}\) bracket force at \(x = 4.5\text{ m}\), eccentricity \(e = 0.5\text{ m}\):
      Equivalent to a \(100\text{ N}\) horizontal force at the beam axis plus a concentrated moment:\[M_{bracket} = 100 \times 0.5 = 50\text{ N·m (CW)} = -50\text{ N·m}\]
  2. Take \(\sum M_Q = 0\) (lever arms measured from \(x_Q = 6.0\text{ m}\)):
    ForceLever Arm (m)SenseMoment (N·m)
    \(V_P\) (up)\(6.0\)CW\(-6.0\, V_P\)
    \(433.013\text{ N}\) (down)\(6.0 - 2.0 = 4.0\)CCW\(+433.013 \times 4.0\)
    \(200\text{ N}\) (up)\(6.0 - 3.5 = 2.5\)CW\(-200 \times 2.5\)
    Bracket moment—CW\(-50\)
    \[-V_P(6.0) + (433.013)(4.0) - (200)(2.5) - 50 = 0\]\[-6.0\,V_P + 1732.052 - 500 - 50 = 0\]\[6.0\,V_P = 1182.052\]\[V_P = \dfrac{1182.052}{6.0} = 197.008\text{ N}\]

4. Final Answer:

\(V_P = \mathbf{197.0\text{ N}}\) | Accepted key range: 195.0 to 200.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q54
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: For the frame shown in the figure (not to scale), all members (AB, BC, CD, GB, and CH) have the same length, \( L \) and flexural rigidity, \( EI \). The joints at B and C are rigid joints, and the supports A and D are fixed supports. Beams GB and CH carry uniformly distributed loads of \( w \) per unit length. The magnitude of the moment reaction at A is \( wL^2/k \). What is the value of \( k \) (in integer)?
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Slope-Deflection Method

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Symmetric portal frame. Supports A & D are fixed. Joints B & C are rigid.
    • All members (AB, BC, CD, GB, CH) have identical length \(L\) and flexural rigidity \(EI\).
    • Cantilever GB (left of B) carries UDL \(w\).
    • Cantilever CH (right of C) carries UDL \(w\).
  • Aim: Determine the magnitude of the moment reaction at fixed support A (\(M_A\)) in the form \(\dfrac{wL^2}{k}\) and find the integer \(k\).

2. Core Concepts:

  • Cantilever Effects: The UDLs on the overhangs transfer moments to joints B and C.
    • Left cantilever GB: \(M_{\text{applied},B} = -\dfrac{wL^2}{2}\) (CCW on joint B)
    • Right cantilever CH: \(M_{\text{applied},C} = +\dfrac{wL^2}{2}\) (CW on joint C)
  • Symmetry: The frame is geometrically symmetric with anti-symmetric nodal moments, so \(\theta_C = -\theta_B\) and there is no lateral sway (\(\Delta = 0\)).

3. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Write Slope-Deflection Equations for Members at Joint B (CW positive):
    • Column BA: \(M_{BA} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}(2\theta_B + \theta_A) = \dfrac{4EI}{L}\theta_B\) (since \(\theta_A = 0\) at fixed support)
    • Beam BC: \(M_{BC} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}(2\theta_B + \theta_C)\)
  2. Apply Joint Equilibrium at Node B:\[M_{BA} + M_{BC} = M_{\text{applied},B}\]\[\dfrac{4EI}{L}\theta_B + \dfrac{2EI}{L}(2\theta_B + \theta_C) = -\dfrac{wL^2}{2}\]\[\dfrac{2EI}{L}(4\theta_B + \theta_C) = -\dfrac{wL^2}{2}\]
  3. Utilize Symmetry (\(\theta_C = -\theta_B\)):\[\dfrac{2EI}{L}(4\theta_B - \theta_B) = -\dfrac{wL^2}{2}\]\[\dfrac{6EI}{L}\theta_B = -\dfrac{wL^2}{2}\]\[\theta_B = -\dfrac{wL^3}{12EI}\]
  4. Calculate Moment Reaction at Support A (\(M_{AB}\)):\[M_{AB} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}(2\theta_A + \theta_B) = \dfrac{2EI}{L}\theta_B\]\[M_{AB} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}\left(-\dfrac{wL^3}{12EI}\right) = -\dfrac{wL^2}{6}\]
    The magnitude of the moment reaction at A is \(\dfrac{wL^2}{6}\).
  5. Determine \(k\):
    Comparing \(\dfrac{wL^2}{6}\) with the given form \(\dfrac{wL^2}{k}\):\[k = 6\]

4. Final Answer:

\(k = \mathbf{6}\) | Accepted key range: 6 to 6

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q55
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question:
Consider the singly reinforced section of a cantilever concrete beam under bending, as shown in the figure (M25 grade concrete, Fe415 grade steel). The stress block parameters for the section at ultimate limit state, as per IS 456: 2000 notations, are given. The ultimate moment of resistance for the section by the Limit State Method is _________________ kN.m (round off to one decimal place).
[Note: Here, \( A_s \) is the total area of tension steel bars, \( b \) is the width of the section, \( d \) is the effective depth of the bars, \( f_{ck} \) is the characteristic compressive cube strength of concrete, \( f_y \) is the yield stress of steel, and \( x_u \) is the depth of neutral axis.]
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | RCC Design (Limit State Method)

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application & Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Concrete Grade: M25 (\(f_{ck} = 25\text{ MPa}\))
    • Steel Grade: Fe415 (\(f_y = 415\text{ MPa}\))
    • Width of section (\(b\)): \(300\text{ mm}\)
    • Tension reinforcement: 3 bars of 28 mm diameter (\(\phi = 28\text{ mm}\))
    • Overall depth (\(D\)): \(600\text{ mm}\)
    • Effective cover (\(d'\)): \(45\text{ mm}\) (from top fiber to centroid of steel, as it is a cantilever under hogging moment)
  • Aim: Calculate the ultimate moment of resistance (\(M_u\)) in \(\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}\) (rounded to one decimal place).

2. Core Concepts:

  • Effective Depth (\(d\)): Distance from extreme compression fiber to centroid of tension reinforcement.\[d = D - \text{effective cover}\]
  • Tensile and Compressive Forces (IS 456:2000, Annex G):\[T = 0.87\, f_y A_{st}, \quad C = 0.36\, f_{ck}\, x_u\, b\]
  • Limiting Neutral Axis: For Fe415, \(x_{u,max} = 0.48\,d\).
  • Ultimate Moment of Resistance:\[M_u = 0.87\, f_y A_{st}\,(d - 0.42\,x_u)\]

3. Solution Method:

Common Pitfall: Many students mistakenly assume \(d = 600\text{ mm}\). However, \(600\text{ mm}\) represents the overall depth \(D\), so \(d = 600 - 45 = 555\text{ mm}\). Using \(d = 600\text{ mm}\) gives \(M_u \approx 331\text{ kN·m}\), which falls outside the official answer key range (295–305).

  1. Calculate the area of steel (\(A_{st}\)).
  2. Calculate \(T\) and find actual \(x_u\) using \(C = T\).
  3. Check if the section is under-reinforced (\(x_u < x_{u,max}\)).
  4. Calculate \(M_u\) using the tension steel lever arm equation.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Effective Depth and Area of Steel:\[d = 600 - 45 = 555\text{ mm}\]\[A_{st} = 3 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times (28)^2 = 3 \times 196\pi = 1847.256\text{ mm}^2\]
  2. Calculate Force and Depth of Neutral Axis (\(x_u\)):\[T = 0.87 \times 415 \times 1847.256 = 666{,}951.785\text{ N}\]Equating \(C = T\):\[0.36 \times 25 \times 300 \times x_u = 666{,}951.785\]\[2700\,x_u = 666{,}951.785 \implies x_u = 247.019\text{ mm}\]
  3. Check Section Type:\[x_{u,max} = 0.48 \times 555 = 266.4\text{ mm}\]Since \(x_u = 247.019\text{ mm} < x_{u,max} = 266.4\text{ mm}\), the section is under-reinforced. The calculation for \(M_u\) based on steel yielding is valid.
  4. Calculate Ultimate Moment of Resistance:\[z = d - 0.42\,x_u = 555 - 0.42(247.019) = 555 - 103.748 = 451.252\text{ mm}\]\[M_u = T \times z = 666{,}951.785 \times 451.252 = 300{,}963{,}326\text{ N·mm}\]\[M_u = \dfrac{300{,}963{,}326}{10^6} \approx 301.0\text{ kN·m}\]

5. Final Answer:

\(M_u = \mathbf{301.0}\text{ kN·m}\) | Accepted key range: 295.0 to 305.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q56
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A 2D thin plate with modulus of elasticity, \( E = 1.0 \) N/m², and Poisson’s ratio, \( \mu = 0.5 \), is in plane stress condition. The displacement field in the plate is given by \( u = Cx^2y \) and \( v = 0 \), where \( u \) and \( v \) are displacements (in m) along the \( X \) and \( Y \) directions, respectively, and \( C \) is a constant (in m⁻²). The distances \( x \) and \( y \) along \( X \) and \( Y \), respectively, are in m. The stress in the \( X \) direction is \( \sigma_{XX} = 40xy \) N/m², and the shear stress is \( \tau_{XY} = \alpha x^2 \) N/m². What is the value of \( \alpha \) (in N/m⁴, in integer)? _________________
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | 2D Plane Stress State

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Modulus of Elasticity: \(E = 1.0\text{ N/m}^2\)
    • Poisson's ratio: \(\mu = 0.5\)
    • Displacements: \(u = Cx^2y,\ v = 0\)
    • Normal stress: \(\sigma_{xx} = 40xy\text{ N/m}^2\)
    • Shear stress: \(\tau_{xy} = \alpha x^2\text{ N/m}^2\)
  • Aim: Find the integer value of the constant \(\alpha\).

2. Core Concepts:

  • Strain-Displacement Relations:\[\epsilon_{xx} = \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x}, \quad \epsilon_{yy} = \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial y}, \quad \gamma_{xy} = \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} + \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial x}\]
  • Generalized Hooke's Law for Plane Stress:\[\sigma_{xx} = \dfrac{E}{1 - \mu^2}(\epsilon_{xx} + \mu\,\epsilon_{yy})\]
  • Shear Modulus and Shear Stress:\[G = \dfrac{E}{2(1+\mu)}, \quad \tau_{xy} = G\,\gamma_{xy}\]

3. Solution Method:

  1. Partially differentiate the displacement field to find \(\epsilon_{xx}\), \(\epsilon_{yy}\), and \(\gamma_{xy}\).
  2. Substitute strains into the plane stress equation to evaluate constant \(C\) using the given \(\sigma_{xx}\).
  3. Calculate the shear modulus \(G\).
  4. Apply the shear stress formula to find \(\tau_{xy}\) in terms of \(x\) and evaluate \(\alpha\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate Strains:\[\epsilon_{xx} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(Cx^2y) = 2Cxy\]\[\epsilon_{yy} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(0) = 0\]\[\gamma_{xy} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(Cx^2y) + 0 = Cx^2\]
  2. Find Constant \(C\):\[\sigma_{xx} = \dfrac{1.0}{1-(0.5)^2}(2Cxy + 0) = \dfrac{1}{0.75}(2Cxy) = \dfrac{8}{3}Cxy\]Given \(\sigma_{xx} = 40xy\):\[\dfrac{8}{3}C = 40 \implies C = \dfrac{40 \times 3}{8} = 15\text{ m}^{-2}\]
  3. Evaluate Shear Modulus and Shear Stress:\[G = \dfrac{1.0}{2(1+0.5)} = \dfrac{1}{3}\text{ N/m}^2\]\[\gamma_{xy} = 15x^2\]\[\tau_{xy} = G\,\gamma_{xy} = \dfrac{1}{3} \times 15x^2 = 5x^2\text{ N/m}^2\]
  4. Determine \(\alpha\):
    Comparing with \(\tau_{xy} = \alpha x^2\):\[\alpha = 5\]

5. Final Answer:

\(\alpha = \mathbf{5}\) | Accepted key range: 5 to 5

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q57
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: An idealised frame supports a load as shown in the figure. The horizontal component of the force transferred from the horizontal member PQ to the vertical member RS at P is _________________ N (round off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Truss & Frame Structures

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Load at Q = \(10\text{ N}\) (downward)
    • PQ is a horizontal member linked to RS at P via a pin.
    • P to U = \(1.2\text{ m}\), U to Q = \(0.6\text{ m}\); overall PQ = \(1.8\text{ m}\).
    • Diagonal strut TU links vertical RS (at T) and horizontal PQ (at U).
    • P to T distance = \(1.0\text{ m}\).
  • Aim: Find the horizontal component of the force transferred from PQ to RS at connection P.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Two-Force Member: Member TU is pinned at both ends with no intermediate loads. It acts purely axially, with its line of action passing exactly through pins T and U.
  • Static Determinacy of Parts: Member PQ is isolated as a Free Body Diagram (FBD). For equilibrium: \(\sum M = 0\) and \(\sum F = 0\).

3. Solution Method:

  1. Recognize TU as a two-force member and use its slope to relate vertical and horizontal components of its reaction force at U.
  2. Take \(\sum M_P = 0\) for member PQ to find vertical reaction at U (\(U_y\)).
  3. Convert \(U_y\) to the horizontal component at U (\(U_x\)).
  4. Apply horizontal equilibrium (\(\sum F_x = 0\)) on member PQ to find horizontal reaction at P (\(P_x\)).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Geometry of Two-Force Member TU:
    Horizontal length \(\Delta x = 1.2\text{ m}\), Vertical drop \(\Delta y = 1.0\text{ m}\).
    By similar triangles (force polygon ∼ geometric slope):\[\dfrac{U_x}{U_y} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta y} = \dfrac{1.2}{1.0} \implies U_x = 1.2\,U_y\]
  2. Moment Equilibrium about P (\(\sum M_P = 0\)):\[U_y \times 1.2 - 10 \times (1.2 + 0.6) = 0\]\[1.2\,U_y = 10 \times 1.8 = 18 \implies U_y = 15\text{ N}\]
  3. Find Horizontal Reaction at U (\(U_x\)):\[U_x = 1.2 \times 15 = 18\text{ N (acting leftward on PQ)}\]
  4. Horizontal Equilibrium for member PQ (\(\sum F_x = 0\)):\[P_x - U_x = 0 \implies P_x = 18\text{ N}\]By Newton's Third Law, the horizontal force transferred to RS at P has magnitude \(18\text{ N}\).

5. Final Answer:

Horizontal component = \(\mathbf{18.0}\text{ N}\) | Accepted key range: 17.5 to 18.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q58
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A square footing is to be designed to carry a column load of 500 kN which is resting on a soil stratum having the following average properties: bulk unit weight = 19 kN/m³; angle of internal friction = 0° and cohesion = 25 kPa.
Considering the depth of the footing as 1 m and adopting Meyerhof’s bearing capacity theory with a factor of safety of 3, the width of the footing (in m) is _________________ (round off to one decimal place)
[Assume the applicable shape and depth factor values as unity; ground water level at greater depth.]
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shallow Foundations

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Type: Square footing
    • Column Load (\(P\)) = \(500\text{ kN}\)
    • Bulk unit weight (\(\gamma\)) = \(19\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Friction angle (\(\phi\)) = \(0^\circ\)
    • Cohesion (\(c\)) = \(25\text{ kPa}\)
    • Depth of footing (\(D_f\)) = \(1\text{ m}\)
    • Factor of Safety (FoS) = \(3\)
    • Meyerhof's theory; Shape and depth factors = \(1.0\); Water table at greater depth (no correction needed).
  • Aim: Calculate the width of the footing \(B\) (in m, rounded to one decimal place).

2. Core Concepts:

  • Meyerhof's Bearing Capacity Equation:\[q_u = c N_c s_c d_c i_c + q N_q s_q d_q i_q + 0.5\,\gamma B N_\gamma s_\gamma d_\gamma i_\gamma\]
  • Bearing Capacity Factors for \(\phi = 0^\circ\): \(N_q = 1.0,\ N_c = 5.14,\ N_\gamma = 0\)
  • Net Safe Bearing Capacity (\(q_{ns}\)):\[q_{nu} = q_u - \gamma D_f, \quad q_{ns} = \dfrac{q_{nu}}{\text{FoS}}\]
  • Sizing the Footing:\[\dfrac{P}{B^2} = q_{ns}\]

3. Solution Method:

  1. Simplify Meyerhof's equation (shape/depth factors = 1.0, \(N_\gamma = 0\)).
  2. Evaluate ultimate bearing capacity (\(q_u\)).
  3. Extract net ultimate (\(q_{nu}\)) and apply FoS to find net safe bearing capacity (\(q_{ns}\)).
  4. Calculate base area required, then take square root to find \(B\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Simplify Bearing Capacity Equation:\[q_u = c N_c + q N_q\]Where \(q = \gamma D_f = 19 \times 1 = 19\text{ kPa}\).
  2. Calculate Ultimate Bearing Capacity:\[q_u = (25 \times 5.14) + (19 \times 1.0) = 128.5 + 19 = 147.5\text{ kPa}\]
  3. Calculate Net Safe Bearing Capacity (\(q_{ns}\)):\[q_{nu} = 147.5 - 19 = 128.5\text{ kPa}\]\[q_{ns} = \dfrac{128.5}{3} = 42.833\text{ kPa}\]
  4. Equate and Find Width (\(B\)):\[\dfrac{500}{B^2} = 42.833 \implies B^2 = \dfrac{500}{42.833} = 11.673\text{ m}^2\]\[B = \sqrt{11.673} = 3.416\text{ m} \approx 3.4\text{ m}\]

5. Final Answer:

\(B = \mathbf{3.4}\text{ m}\) | Accepted key range: 3.0 to 3.5

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q59
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question:
A circular pile of diameter 0.6 m and length 8 m was constructed in a cohesive soil stratum having the following properties: bulk unit weight = 19 kN/m³; angle of internal friction = 0° and cohesion = 25 kPa.
The allowable load the pile can carry with a factor of safety of 3 is _________________ kN (round off to one decimal place).
[Adopt: Adhesion factor, \( \alpha = 1.0 \) and Bearing capacity factor, \( N_c = 9.0 \)]
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Deep Foundations

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Diameter of circular pile: \(D = 0.6\text{ m}\)
    • Length of pile: \(L = 8\text{ m}\)
    • Bulk unit weight: \(\gamma = 19\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Angle of internal friction: \(\phi = 0^\circ\)
    • Cohesion: \(c = 25\text{ kPa}\)
    • Factor of Safety: \(FOS = 3\)
    • Adhesion factor: \(\alpha = 1.0\)
    • Bearing capacity factor: \(N_c = 9.0\)
  • Aim: Determine the allowable load (\(Q_{allow}\)) the pile can carry in kN.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Ultimate Bearing Capacity (\(Q_u\)):\[Q_u = Q_p + Q_s\]
  • End Bearing (\(Q_p\)):\[Q_p = c \cdot N_c \cdot A_b\]where \(A_b\) is the cross-sectional area of the pile base.
  • Skin Friction (\(Q_s\)):\[Q_s = \alpha \cdot \bar{c} \cdot A_s\]where \(A_s\) is the surface area of the pile shaft.
  • Allowable Load:\[Q_{allow} = \dfrac{Q_u}{FOS}\]

3. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate base area (\(A_b\)) and shaft surface area (\(A_s\)).
  2. Compute point bearing resistance (\(Q_p\)) and frictional resistance (\(Q_s\)).
  3. Sum to find ultimate load capacity (\(Q_u\)).
  4. Apply the Factor of Safety to compute \(Q_{allow}\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate geometrical properties of the pile:\[A_b = \dfrac{\pi}{4}D^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}(0.6)^2 = 0.28274\text{ m}^2\]\[A_s = \pi D L = \pi(0.6)(8) = 15.0796\text{ m}^2\]
  2. Calculate Ultimate End Bearing Capacity (\(Q_p\)):\[Q_p = 25 \times 9.0 \times 0.28274 = 63.617\text{ kN}\]
  3. Calculate Ultimate Skin Friction Resistance (\(Q_s\)):\[Q_s = 1.0 \times 25 \times 15.0796 = 376.99\text{ kN}\]
  4. Calculate Total Ultimate Load (\(Q_u\)):\[Q_u = 63.617 + 376.99 = 440.607\text{ kN}\]
  5. Calculate Allowable Load (\(Q_{allow}\)):\[Q_{allow} = \dfrac{440.607}{3} = 146.869 \approx 146.9\text{ kN}\]

5. Final Answer:

\(Q_{allow} = \mathbf{146.9}\text{ kN}\) | Accepted key range: 145.0 to 149.0

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q60
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: For the flow setup shown in the figure (not to scale), the hydraulic conductivities of the two soil samples, Soil 1 and Soil 2, are 10 mm/s and 1 mm/s, respectively. Assume the unit weight of water as 10 kN/m³ and ignore the velocity head. At steady state, what is the total head (in m, rounded off to two decimal places) at any point located at the junction of the two samples? _________________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Permeability & Seepage

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Hydraulic conductivity of Soil 1: \(k_1 = 10\text{ mm/s}\)
    • Hydraulic conductivity of Soil 2: \(k_2 = 1\text{ mm/s}\)
    • Length of Soil 1 (elev. 3 m to 2 m): \(L_1 = 1\text{ m}\)
    • Length of Soil 2 (elev. 2 m to 1 m): \(L_2 = 1\text{ m}\)
    • Pressure on top water surface (elev. 4 m): \(P = 10\text{ kPa}\)
    • Unit weight of water: \(\gamma_w = 10\text{ kN/m}^3\)
    • Bottom water surface elevation: \(0\text{ m}\)
    • Velocity head is ignored.
  • Aim: Find the total head (\(H_{junction}\)) at the junction of the two samples (elevation 2 m).

2. Core Concepts:

  • Total Head (\(H\)):\[H = \dfrac{P}{\gamma_w} + Z\]
  • Continuity Equation for 1D Seepage: In steady state, discharge velocity is constant across series soil layers.\[v = k_1 i_1 = k_2 i_2, \quad i_1 = \dfrac{\Delta H_1}{L_1},\ i_2 = \dfrac{\Delta H_2}{L_2}\]

3. Solution Method:

  1. Establish boundary conditions for total head at top and bottom of the soil system.
  2. Equate flow velocities in both soil layers.
  3. Solve for the unknown total head at the junction (\(H_{junction}\)).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total Head at Top Boundary (\(H_{top}\)):
    Top water surface at \(Z = 4\text{ m}\), pressure head \(= \dfrac{10}{10} = 1\text{ m}\).\[H_{top} = 4 + 1 = 5\text{ m}\]Since water is continuous from 4 m to 3 m, total head at the top of Soil 1 (elev. 3 m) remains \(5\text{ m}\).
  2. Total Head at Bottom Boundary (\(H_{bot}\)):
    Bottom free surface at \(Z = 0\text{ m}\), \(P = 0\).\[H_{bot} = 0 + 0 = 0\text{ m}\]
  3. Apply Continuity Equation:
    Let \(H_{junction}\) be the total head at elevation 2 m.
    Head loss across Soil 1: \(\Delta H_1 = 5 - H_{junction}\)
    Head loss across Soil 2: \(\Delta H_2 = H_{junction} - 0 = H_{junction}\)\[k_1\dfrac{\Delta H_1}{L_1} = k_2\dfrac{\Delta H_2}{L_2}\]\[10 \times \dfrac{5 - H_{junction}}{1} = 1 \times \dfrac{H_{junction}}{1}\]\[50 - 10\,H_{junction} = H_{junction}\]\[11\,H_{junction} = 50 \implies H_{junction} = \dfrac{50}{11} = 4.5\overline{45}\text{ m}\]
  4. Rounding Off: \(H_{junction} \approx 4.55\text{ m}\)

5. Final Answer:

\(H_{junction} = \mathbf{4.55}\text{ m}\) | Accepted key range: 4.50 to 4.60

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q61
questions.subject: Geotechnical Engineering (Soil)
questions.question: A consolidated drained (CD) triaxial test was carried out on a sand sample with the known effective shear strength parameters, \( c' = 0 \) and \( \phi' = 30^\circ \). In the test, prior to the failure, when the sample was undergoing axial compression under constant cell pressure, the drainage valve was accidentally closed. At the failure, 360 kPa deviatoric stress was recorded along with 70 kPa pore water pressure. If the test is repeated without such error, and no back pressure is applied in either of the tests, what is the deviatoric stress (in kPa, in integer) at the failure? _________________
questions.explanation:
Geotechnical Engineering | Shear Strength of Soil

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Sand sample effective shear strength parameters: \(c' = 0\text{ kPa}\), \(\phi' = 30^\circ\)
    • Test 1: Intended as CD, but drainage valve accidentally closed prior to failure. Constant cell pressure maintained.
      • Deviatoric stress at failure: \(q_{f1} = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)_{f1} = 360\text{ kPa}\)
      • Pore water pressure at failure: \(u_f = 70\text{ kPa}\)
    • Test 2: Correctly repeated as CD test (no accidental valve closure \(\implies u = 0\)). No back pressure applied in either test.
  • Aim: Find the deviatoric stress (\(q_{f2}\)) at failure in Test 2.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Effective Stress Principle: \(\sigma' = \sigma - u\)
  • Mohr-Coulomb Failure Criterion for \(c' = 0\):\[\sigma_1' = \sigma_3'\tan^2\!\left(45^\circ + \dfrac{\phi'}{2}\right)\]
  • Deviatoric Stress: \(q = \sigma_1 - \sigma_3 = \sigma_1' - \sigma_3'\)

3. Solution Method:

  1. Use failure conditions of Test 1 to find effective cell pressure (\(\sigma_3'\)) and total cell pressure (\(\sigma_3\)).
  2. Recognize the same total cell pressure (\(\sigma_3\)) is used in Test 2.
  3. For Test 2 (true CD test), pore pressure is zero, so total stresses equal effective stresses.
  4. Apply the failure criterion to find \(\sigma_1'\) and compute \(q_{f2}\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Analyze Test 1 to find cell pressure (\(\sigma_3\)):\[N_\phi = \tan^2\!\left(45^\circ + \dfrac{30^\circ}{2}\right) = \tan^2(60^\circ) = 3\]At failure in Test 1: \(\sigma_1' = 3\sigma_3'\)\[q_{f1} = \sigma_1' - \sigma_3' = 3\sigma_3' - \sigma_3' = 2\sigma_3' = 360\text{ kPa}\]\[\sigma_3' = 180\text{ kPa}\]Total cell pressure:\[\sigma_3 = \sigma_3' + u_f = 180 + 70 = 250\text{ kPa}\]
  2. Analyze Test 2 (True CD Test):
    Same constant total cell pressure: \(\sigma_3 = 250\text{ kPa}\).
    Excess pore pressure fully dissipates, so \(u = 0\):\[\sigma_3' = \sigma_3 = 250\text{ kPa}\]
  3. Calculate Deviatoric Stress for Test 2:\[\sigma_1' = 3 \times 250 = 750\text{ kPa}\]\[q_{f2} = \sigma_1' - \sigma_3' = 750 - 250 = 500\text{ kPa}\]

5. Final Answer:

\(q_{f2} = \mathbf{500}\text{ kPa}\) | Accepted key range: 500 to 500

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q62
questions.subject: Water Resources & Hydraulics
questions.question:
A catchment may be idealized as a circle of radius 30 km. There are five rain gauges, one at the center of the catchment and four on the boundary (equi-spaced), as shown in the figure (not to scale).
The annual rainfall recorded at these gauges in a particular year are given below.
GaugeG₁G₂G₃G₄G₅
Rainfall (mm)910930925895905

Using the Thiessen polygon method, what is the average rainfall (in mm, rounded off to two decimal places) over the catchment in that year? _________________
questions.explanation:
Hydrology | Precipitation & Mean Areal Rainfall

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Catchment shape: Circle with radius \(R = 30\text{ km}\)
    • 5 Rain gauges: \(G_1\) at the center; \(G_2, G_3, G_4, G_5\) on the boundary, equi-spaced (\(90^\circ\) apart).
    • Rainfall records: \(P_1 = 910\text{ mm}\), \(P_2 = 930\text{ mm}\), \(P_3 = 925\text{ mm}\), \(P_4 = 895\text{ mm}\), \(P_5 = 905\text{ mm}\)
  • Aim: Calculate the average rainfall over the catchment using the Thiessen polygon method.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Thiessen Polygon Method: Assigns an area (weight) to each gauge. Polygons are constructed by drawing perpendicular bisectors to lines connecting adjacent gauges.
  • Average Rainfall (\(\bar{P}\)):\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{\sum(A_i P_i)}{\sum A_i} = \sum(W_i P_i)\]where \(W_i = \dfrac{A_i}{A_{total}}\).

3. Solution Method:

  1. Establish the geometry to find the area represented by the central gauge (\(G_1\)).
  2. Determine the area represented by the four outer gauges (\(G_2\) to \(G_5\)) using symmetry.
  3. Calculate the respective weights (\(W_i\)) for each gauge.
  4. Compute the weighted average rainfall.

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Total Catchment Area:\[A_{total} = \pi R^2\]
  2. Polygon Area for Central Gauge (\(G_1\)):
    With \(G_1\) at origin and outer gauges at \((0,R),\ (R,0),\ (0,-R),\ (-R,0)\), the perpendicular bisectors of lines from \(G_1\) to each outer gauge form the lines \(y = \pm R/2\) and \(x = \pm R/2\) — a square of side \(R\).\[A_1 = R \times R = R^2\](The square lies entirely within the circular catchment since the maximum distance from center to corner is \(R/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707R < R\).)
  3. Polygon Areas for Outer Gauges (\(G_2\) to \(G_5\)):\[\text{Remaining Area} = \pi R^2 - R^2 = R^2(\pi - 1)\]\[A_{outer} = \dfrac{R^2(\pi-1)}{4} \quad \text{(by symmetry)}\]
  4. Calculate Thiessen Weights:\[W_1 = \dfrac{R^2}{\pi R^2} = \dfrac{1}{\pi} \approx 0.31831\]\[W_{outer} = \dfrac{(\pi-1)/4}{\pi} = \dfrac{\pi-1}{4\pi} \approx 0.17042\]Check: \(\dfrac{1}{\pi} + 4 \times \dfrac{\pi-1}{4\pi} = \dfrac{1 + \pi - 1}{\pi} = 1.0\) ✓
  5. Compute Average Rainfall (\(\bar{P}\)):\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\times 910 + \dfrac{\pi-1}{4\pi}\times(930 + 925 + 895 + 905)\]\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{910}{\pi} + \dfrac{(\pi-1)\times 3655}{4\pi}\]\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{3640 + 3655\pi - 3655}{4\pi} = \dfrac{3655\pi - 15}{4\pi}\]\[\bar{P} = \dfrac{3655}{4} - \dfrac{15}{4\pi} = 913.75 - 1.1937 = 912.556...\text{ mm}\]

5. Final Answer:

\(\bar{P} = \mathbf{912.56}\text{ mm}\) | Accepted key range: 912.28 to 912.82

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q64
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question:
The theoretical aerobic oxidation of biomass (C₅H₇O₂N) is given below:
C₅H₇O₂N + 5O₂ → 5CO₂ + NH₃ + 2H₂O
The biochemical oxidation of biomass is assumed as a first-order reaction with a rate constant of 0.23/d at 20°C (logarithm to base e). Neglecting the second-stage oxygen demand from its biochemical oxidation, the ratio of BOD₅ at 20°C to total organic carbon (TOC) of biomass is _________________ (round off to two decimal places).
[Consider the atomic weights of C, H, O and N as 12 g/mol, 1 g/mol, 16 g/mol and 14 g/mol, respectively]
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Wastewater Quality (BOD Kinetics)

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Biomass reaction: \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_7\text{O}_2\text{N} + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 5\text{CO}_2 + \text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)
    • First-order BOD rate constant at 20°C: \(k = 0.23\text{ d}^{-1}\) (base \(e\))
    • Second-stage (nitrogenous) oxygen demand is neglected.
    • Atomic weights: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16, N = 14 g/mol
  • Aim: Find the ratio \(BOD_5 / TOC\) of the biomass.

2. Core Concepts:

  • Total Organic Carbon (TOC): Mass of elemental carbon present in a given molecule.
  • Ultimate Carbonaceous BOD (\(L_0\)): Theoretical oxygen demand for the carbonaceous stage only. From the balanced equation, 1 mole of biomass demands 5 moles of \(\text{O}_2\).
  • First-Order BOD Kinetics:\[BOD_t = L_0\left(1 - e^{-k\cdot t}\right)\]

3. Solution Method:

  1. Calculate the mass of Carbon in 1 mole of biomass (TOC).
  2. Find the mass of \(\text{O}_2\) required for 1 mole of biomass (Ultimate CBOD, \(L_0\)).
  3. Apply BOD kinetics to find \(BOD_5\) over 5 days.
  4. Compute the ratio \(BOD_5 / TOC\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Calculate TOC:\[\text{TOC} = 5 \times 12 = 60\text{ g/mol}\]
  2. Calculate Ultimate Carbonaceous BOD (\(L_0\)):
    From stoichiometry, 1 mole of biomass reacts with 5 moles of \(\text{O}_2\):\[L_0 = 5 \times 32 = 160\text{ g/mol}\]
  3. Calculate \(BOD_5\) at 20°C:\[BOD_5 = 160 \times \left(1 - e^{-0.23 \times 5}\right) = 160 \times \left(1 - e^{-1.15}\right)\]\[BOD_5 = 160 \times (1 - 0.316637) = 160 \times 0.683363 = 109.338\text{ g/mol}\]
  4. Calculate the Ratio:\[\dfrac{BOD_5}{\text{TOC}} = \dfrac{109.338}{60} = 1.8223 \approx 1.82\]

5. Final Answer:

\(\dfrac{BOD_5}{TOC} = \mathbf{1.82}\) | Accepted key range: 1.80 to 2.00

questions.title: GATE CE 2023 Set 2 | CE Q65
questions.subject: Environmental Engineering
questions.question: A system of seven river segments is shown in the schematic diagram. The Rᵢ's, Qᵢ's, and Cᵢ's (i = 1 to 7) are the river segments, their corresponding flow rates, and concentrations of a conservative pollutant, respectively. Assume complete mixing at the intersections, no additional water loss or gain in the system, and steady state condition. Given: Q₁ = 5 m³/s ; Q₂ = 15 m³/s ; Q₄ = 3 m³/s ; Q₆ = 8 m³/s ; C₁ = 8 kg/m³ ; C₂ = 12 kg/m³ ; C₆ = 10 kg/m³. What is the steady state concentration (in kg/m³, rounded off to two decimal place) of the pollutant in the river segment 7? _________________
questions.explanation:
Environmental Engineering | Water Quality & River Mixing

1. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • \(Q_1 = 5\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(C_1 = 8\text{ kg/m}^3\)
    • \(Q_2 = 15\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(C_2 = 12\text{ kg/m}^3\)
    • \(Q_4 = 3\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\) (diverted/extracted flow from \(R_3\))
    • \(Q_6 = 8\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\), \(C_6 = 10\text{ kg/m}^3\)
    • Conservative pollutant (no decay), complete mixing at junctions, steady state.
  • Aim: Find the steady-state concentration \(C_7\) in segment \(R_7\) (in kg/m³).

2. Core Concepts:

  • Continuity Equation (Flow Balance):\[\sum Q_{in} = \sum Q_{out}\]
  • Mass Balance Equation:\[\sum(Q_{in} \cdot C_{in}) = \sum(Q_{out} \cdot C_{out})\]
  • Flow Split Principle: When a uniformly mixed stream (\(R_3\)) splits into branches (\(R_4\) and \(R_5\)), the concentration is identical in each branch: \(C_4 = C_5 = C_3\).

3. Solution Method:

  1. Node 1 (\(R_1 + R_2 \rightarrow R_3\)): Flow and mass balance to find \(Q_3\) and \(C_3\).
  2. Node 2 (\(R_3 \rightarrow R_4 + R_5\)): Flow balance to find \(Q_5\); concentration unchanged by split.
  3. Node 3 (\(R_5 + R_6 \rightarrow R_7\)): Flow and mass balance to find \(Q_7\) and \(C_7\).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Node 1: \(R_1 + R_2 \rightarrow R_3\)
    Flow Balance:\[Q_3 = Q_1 + Q_2 = 5 + 15 = 20\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\]Mass Balance:\[20 \times C_3 = (5 \times 8) + (15 \times 12) = 40 + 180 = 220\text{ kg/s}\]\[C_3 = \dfrac{220}{20} = 11\text{ kg/m}^3\]
  2. Node 2: \(R_3 \rightarrow R_4 + R_5\)
    Flow Balance:\[Q_5 = Q_3 - Q_4 = 20 - 3 = 17\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\]Concentration (split does not alter concentration):\[C_5 = C_4 = C_3 = 11\text{ kg/m}^3\]
  3. Node 3: \(R_5 + R_6 \rightarrow R_7\)
    Flow Balance:\[Q_7 = Q_5 + Q_6 = 17 + 8 = 25\text{ m}^3/\text{s}\]Mass Balance:\[25 \times C_7 = (17 \times 11) + (8 \times 10) = 187 + 80 = 267\text{ kg/s}\]\[C_7 = \dfrac{267}{25} = 10.68\text{ kg/m}^3\]

5. Final Answer:

\(C_7 = \mathbf{10.68}\text{ kg/m}^3\) | Accepted key range: 10.58 to 10.78
